articles.title: I built a CLI harness that strips JS/TS function bodies with Babel AST to save 80% context tokens
articles.excerpt: While working on large Next.js and TypeScript repositories, I noticed AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code) constantly burning through context limits. They were reading 500-line implementation files…
articles.body: While working on large Next.js and TypeScript repositories, I noticed AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code) constantly burning through context limits. They were reading 500-line implementation files when all they really needed were the types, interfaces, and exported signatures. To solve this mechanically, I engineered and open-sourced Apex Agents. How It Works: Babel AST Compactor ( npx apex-agents compact ): Parses TypeScript, JSX, and JavaScript using @babel/parser and replaces function bodies with {} while preserving all types, generics, parameters, and exports. In our tests, an ~13k token codebase compacted down to ~1.4k tokens (88.5% reduction) into an APEX_CONTEXT.md file.
articles.author: AmanullaShaikh

articles.title: Rolling Out Passkeys Without Locking Users Out
articles.excerpt: The first time I shipped passkeys for a client's SaaS dashboard, sign-in worked perfectly on staging and failed for about 30% of users on production for two days. Nothing was wrong with the cryptograp…
articles.body: The first time I shipped passkeys for a client's SaaS dashboard, sign-in worked perfectly on staging and failed for about 30% of users on production for two days. Nothing was wrong with the cryptography. Production served the login page from app.example.com , but the backend verified responses against an RP ID and origin configured as example.com and https://example.com . Chrome users on one path were fine; users who registered through the marketing site's embedded flow were not. Every failure looked the same in the logs: "verification failed". Passkeys are the best login upgrade most web apps can make right now, but the rollout details decide whether users love them or get locked out.
articles.author: Muhammad Ali Mughal

articles.title: The Prediction Succeeded. The CLI Still Failed.
articles.excerpt: A prediction routine returned a valid result. The command then failed before it could save that result. This happened in spec-lane, a CLI I maintain that can estimate token usage for AI-assisted devel…
articles.body: A prediction routine returned a valid result. The command then failed before it could save that result. This happened in spec-lane , a CLI I maintain that can estimate token usage for AI-assisted development from previous observations. The command ran two related paths: estimate/v2 , which selects observations with matching conditions, followed by a v1 estimator over a broader population. The second path could throw even after the first had produced a prediction. The surprising part was an assumption in the error handler: because v2's population was a subset of v1's, a v1 failure supposedly meant v2 must also have abstained. That does not follow when the two paths select their nearest neighbors from different populations. Eight observations worked. Twelve did not.

articles.title: How Does Discord Work?
articles.excerpt: TL;DR Discord runs text and voice as separate systems, because messages must never be lost but audio can’t wait. Text goes through an HTTPS API and a Gateway WebSocket. Messages are stored in ScyllaDB…
articles.body: TL;DR Discord runs text and voice as separate systems, because messages must never be lost but audio can’t wait. Text goes through an HTTPS API and a Gateway WebSocket. Messages are stored in ScyllaDB, which replaced Cassandra in 2022. Voice setup uses a WebSocket, and the audio travels over UDP through a selective forwarding unit (SFU) that copies packets to everyone in the call. Since March 2026, calls are end-to-end encrypted with the DAVE protocol. Text is not. Before Discord, talking to friends while you played a game took real effort. Like, being in the same room as them! Or you could use voice chat services like TeamSpeak, Ventrilo, or Mumble. But that meant someone in the group had to rent or run a server and hand out an IP address and port.

articles.title: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
articles.excerpt: Celestron’s StarSense Explorer tech makes this 150mm Dobsonian so easy to operate — but its tabletop design makes me wonder whether beginners should go bigger.
articles.body: Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope. Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

articles.excerpt: Let’s get to work. | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Normally, the products I test don't offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic's AI agent fo…
articles.body: Let’s get to work. | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Normally, the products I test don't offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic's AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don't write code. It's been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant , Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things , and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots . Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those. articles.title: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX
articles.excerpt: SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented double-catch mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.
articles.body: Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030. SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship 's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.
articles.author: Andrew Jones

articles.title: Powerful Vulcan Centaur rocket launching for 1st time in 9 months Nov. 14: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket will launch 40 Amazon internet satellites to orbit on Nov. 14. You can watch the liftoff — Vulcan's first since February —live here at Space.com.
articles.body: Update: United Launch Alliance has delayed the launch of its Vulcan Centaur rocket to Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT) due to a power issue in a liquid gaseous nitrogen factory that pumps propellant into the rocket. "The vehicle and spacecraft are healthy," ULA wrote in an update on X. United Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket will fly on Saturday (Nov. 14) for the first time in nine months, and you can watch the action live. A Vulcan Centaur topped with 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites is scheduled to lift off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the company . Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff.

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.excerpt: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Me…
articles.body: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision.
articles.author: Aaron Zamost
